guide.disclaimer: This sound player is an educational and wellness tool. It is not intended as medical therapy for chronic insomnia, tinnitus, or clinical sensory processing disorders. Consult a healthcare professional if sleep difficulties persist.
guide.physicsDesc: Acoustic noise is characterized by its power spectral density across audible frequencies (20 Hz to 20,000 Hz). The mathematical formula P(f) = 1/f^α defines the spectral slope and perceptual warmth of each color of noise.
guide.whiteDesc: Equal energy across all audible frequencies. Resembles television static or an air conditioner; provides broad acoustic masking against irregular environmental disruptions.
guide.pinkDesc: Power drops by 3 dB per octave. Aligns closely with human cochlear sensitivity and natural rhythms (rainfall, gentle wind). Research associates pink noise with enhanced slow-wave sleep and memory consolidation.
guide.brownDesc: Power drops by 6 dB per octave, producing deep, low-frequency warmth similar to roaring ocean surf or distant thunder. Highly favored for rapid relaxation and reducing nervous arousal.
guide.maskingDesc: Continuous stationary noise smooths acoustic contrast, preventing sudden auditory cortex arousal spikes caused by erratic ambient noises (doors, sirens, traffic).
guide.resonanceDesc: Nonlinear background acoustic energy can elevate sub-threshold neural signals in the prefrontal cortex, enhancing cognitive performance, task attention, and working memory.
guide.hygieneDesc: Maintain sound output below 60 dBA at ear level, position speakers at least 1.5 meters away from the bed, and utilize the sleep timer for optimal rest transitions.
guide.faq1Q: Q: What is the difference between white, pink, and brown noise?
guide.faq1A: A: The difference is spectral energy distribution. White noise has equal energy across all frequencies, pink noise decreases by 3 dB per octave for a natural soothing balance, and brown noise drops by 6 dB per octave with rich low-frequency depth for deep sleep.
guide.faq2Q: Q: How does sound masking prevent nighttime awakenings?
guide.faq2A: A: Sudden ambient sounds trigger micro-arousals in the brain. A continuous soundscape raises the baseline auditory threshold, masking transient noise spikes and stabilizing sleep cycles.
guide.faq3Q: Q: Can ambient noise help people with ADHD or focus issues?
guide.faq3A: A: Yes. Through stochastic resonance, optimal levels of acoustic background noise help dopamine-deficient individuals modulate arousal levels and maintain sustained attention during cognitive tasks.
guide.faq4Q: Q: What is the recommended volume and speaker placement?
guide.faq4A: A: Keep volume below 60 dBA (quiet conversational level) at ear level and place speakers 1.5 to 2 meters (5 to 7 feet) away from your bed. Use the built-in timer to avoid unnecessary all-night exposure.
